events.title: East India Company rule
hints: A chartered trading corporation governed a subcontinent with its own private army.
A victory at Plassey in 1757 opened the door to rule.
A great rebellion in 1857 ended its rule.
events.summary: Following victory at Plassey in 1757 the English East India Company became the ruling power across large parts of the subcontinent, collecting land revenue and controlling trade in cotton textiles, indigo and opium. The Crown took over after the 1857 rebellion.
events.quip: The only time a shareholder meeting came with an army and a tax code.

events.title: The British Raj
hints: Rule passed from a trading company to the Crown in 1858.
Its viceroys governed from Calcutta and then a purpose-built new capital.
Independence arrived in 1947 together with a painful partition.
events.summary: From 1858 the subcontinent was governed directly by the British Crown. Raw cotton, tea, indigo and opium flowed to Britain and its markets, while local industries such as handloom textiles declined and recurrent famines took many lives.

events.title: Bengal famine of 1943
hints: A wartime famine struck a rice-growing province after a cyclone and the loss of imports.
Grain exports and requisitions continued while people starved.
events.summary: An estimated two to three million people died in Bengal in 1943 and 1944. A cyclone, crop disease and the loss of Burmese rice imports triggered the shortage, and wartime policies of the British government, including requisitions, denial policies and continued exports, worsened it.

events.title: Portuguese Goa
hints: A coastal enclave held by a European crown for more than four centuries.
It outlasted every other European foothold on the subcontinent and ended only in 1961.
events.summary: Portugal captured Goa in 1510 and made it the capital of its eastern empire, controlling the spice trade routes. It was the last European colony on the subcontinent, taken by a military operation in December 1961.

events.title: Timur's sack of Delhi
hints: A Central Asian conqueror crossed the Indus at the end of the fourteenth century.
He sacked the Delhi Sultanate's capital in December 1398.
Captive craftsmen were taken to his capital in Samarkand.
events.summary: Timur crossed the Indus in 1398 and defeated the Delhi Sultanate's army. The sack of Delhi in December 1398 was followed by massacres and the looting of the city. Skilled artisans and large amounts of plunder were taken to Samarkand.

events.title: Nader Shah's invasion and the Peacock Throne
hints: A Persian ruler marched through the Khyber Pass in 1738.
A massacre in the capital in March 1739 followed a street riot.
The Peacock Throne and a famous diamond were carried away.
events.summary: In 1738 and 1739 Nader Shah of Persia invaded the Mughal Empire and defeated its army at Karnal. His troops sacked Delhi in March 1739, killing many thousands, and carried off the Peacock Throne, the Koh-i-Noor diamond and a treasury of immense value.

events.title: French India
hints: A handful of coastal towns remained under another European flag for nearly three centuries.
Pondicherry was the capital of the French establishments.
Chandernagore voted to merge in 1949 and the rest followed in 1954.
events.summary: France founded Pondicherry in 1674, and its trading posts at Chandernagore, Karikal, Mahé and Yanam survived long after the Seven Years' War ended its hopes of empire. They were exploited mainly as ports and textile centres and were transferred in the 1950s.

events.title: The Great Hedge of India
hints: A customs barrier made largely of thorny plants stretched across half a subcontinent.
It existed to enforce a tax on a kitchen staple.
At its peak it ran for thousands of kilometres from the north-west to the Bay of Bengal.
events.summary: To stop salt being smuggled untaxed from coastal regions, the East India Company and later the Crown built the Inland Customs Line, often a barrier of thorny hedge, patrolled by thousands of officers, which extended for over 2,500 miles. It was abolished in 1879 when salt duties were equalised.
events.quip: A 4,000-kilometre thorn hedge, built because collecting salt tax by shrubbery seemed reasonable.

events.title: Great Famine of 1876 to 1878
hints: A prolonged drought struck southern and western provinces in the 1870s.
A grand imperial assemblage was held at Delhi in 1877 as the famine raged.
Grain exports continued and relief policy was dictated by a belief in minimal intervention.
events.summary: A severe drought brought famine to Madras, Bombay, Mysore and Hyderabad in 1876 to 1878, with millions dying. Historians criticise colonial relief policy, which prioritised budget limits and the free movement of grain over feeding the starving.

events.title: Partition of British India
hints: A boundary was drawn in weeks by a lawyer who had never visited the region.
The Radcliffe Line split Punjab and Bengal.
Millions crossed new borders in the largest migration of the century.
events.summary: In 1947 the British withdrew from the subcontinent in haste and partitioned it into India and Pakistan. The Radcliffe boundary awards split Punjab and Bengal; an estimated 10 to 20 million people were displaced and several hundred thousand to two million died in the violence.
